title: Compound growth, explained with $100 a month

scenes.heading: Compound growth, explained with $100 a month
scenes.narration: Compound growth sounds complicated. It isn't. Let's walk through it with $100 a month.

scenes.heading: Growth on growth
scenes.narration: Compound growth means your gains can earn gains of their own. If an investment grows this year, next year that growth can grow too. Over many years, that adds up, which is why time matters so much.
scenes.on_screen:
Gains can earn gains
The effect builds over the years

scenes.heading: $100 a month, two start dates
scenes.narration: Here's a hypothetical. One person puts in $100 a month from age 25. Another starts at 30. Both assume a steady 6% a year. By 65, the early starter has put in $48,000, and the balance could be about $191,700. The later starter could have about $138,000. Waiting five years means $6,000 less put in, but about $53,700 less at the end.

chart.note: Hypothetical: $100 added at the start of each month, 6% a year compounded monthly, ages 25 to 65. Not a prediction.

scenes.heading: The catch
scenes.narration: Now the catch. Real markets don't move in a smooth line like this chart. Some years they fall, sometimes a lot, and recovering can take years. A steady 6% is a simplification, not a promise.
scenes.on_screen:
Real markets go up and down
Some years they fall a lot
Growth is never promised

scenes.heading: Recap
scenes.narration: Quick recap. Growth can earn growth of its own over time. Starting earlier gives money more years to grow. And growth is never promised. Examples are hypothetical. Investments can fall in value, including the money you put in.
scenes.on_screen:
Gains can earn gains
Earlier means more years
Growth is never promised
